To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of different identical names for biosimilars is unwarranted and would be detrimental to the public interest.

the FDA’s current naming system is scientifically sound, that there is no need to change it, and that the FDA should continue to use the same non-proprietary or generic names to identify both the reference product and the biosimilar product.
FDA should not adopt a policy of using different identical non- proprietary names to identify biosimilar and interchangeable products.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and naming of biologic products in the United States.
the question of whether the FDA should require biosimilar products to bear a different non-proprietary, or generic, name than their corresponding reference product.
the question of whether FDA should permit the use of different identical names for reference products and their “highly similar,” biosimilar and interchangeable counterparts.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is no evidence of any need for use of differential identical names to identify biosimilar and reference products, and that the use of such differential names would be contrary to the legislative purpose and the statutory mandate of the Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act of 2009.

there is no evidence, and no need, to use different identical non-­proprietary names for the “highly ­similar” active drug substance of reference biologic and its corresponding biosimilar or interchangeable product.
the use of differential identical names is not scientifically justified, is not needed to meet any legitimate regulatory need, and will impede access to affordable biosimilars.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the FDA should not adopt a new, non-proprietary naming policy that would require biosimilares to bear different non-proprietary product names than those assigned to the reference product, and that FDA should not adopt any policy that would require use of non-proprietary ingredient names different from the non-proprietary active ingredient name assigned by the World Health Organization.
FDA should continue to use the same identical non-propriety name for a biosimilar and its reference product, and that the reference product name should be the non-proprietary, or generic, name.

the use of different identical names for the “highly” similar drug substance of a reference product and its biosimilar is unwarranted and unnecessary, and will impede access to safe, affordable, and effective biologic medicines for millions of patients in need.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the FDA has a responsibility to ensure that the public is not harmed by any new naming scheme.
FDA should reject differential identical non- proprietary naming and should instead adopt the solution that has been proposed.
the use of different names will create confusion, and that the FDA should not require it.
